name: Copper
toxicityNote: Copper can leach into liquids and tarnish to green salts; avoid elixirs, avoid dust and wash hands after handling raw specimens.

Kept nearby for warmth and stamina
Folk traditions link copper jewelry to comfort
summary: Native copper is the pure orange metal found as branching crystals and nuggets, used in tradition as a conductor of energy, warmth and steady vitality.
intro: Native copper is copper in its raw, natural form: bright orange when fresh, darkening to brown and then green as it weathers. It grows in branching, tree-like or wiry crystal forms, in nuggets and as sheets filling cracks in volcanic rock. The Keweenaw Peninsula of Michigan is world famous for huge masses of native copper, some weighing many tons. At 2.5 to 3 it is soft and malleable, and conducts heat and electricity extremely well. Crystal lovers treasure it as a stone-metal, a warm conductor that links other stones and the body.
history: Copper was one of the first metals used by humans, with worked native copper dating back about 10,000 years in Anatolia. In North America, the Old Copper Complex peoples of the Great Lakes hammered native copper into tools and ornaments for thousands of years. The Bronze Age took its name from copper alloyed with tin. The metal was associated with Venus in alchemy, and with Cyprus, from which the name derives. Egyptians used it for mirrors, tools and jewelry. In crystal healing, copper wire and native copper pieces are used with stones to carry intention.
meaning: Crystal practitioners regard copper as a conductor of energy. Whether as raw native copper or as wire wraps, it is said to amplify the properties of stones it touches and to help energy flow. It is linked to the sacral and heart chakras, with associations to warmth, relationships and vitality. Emotionally it is said to warm cold moods and encourage open expression. Many people wear copper jewelry as a comforting accessory, and folk tradition links copper bracelets with ease in the joints and warmth, though this is not medical advice. Native copper specimens are prized for their natural, branching beauty and their connection to the Earth.
howToUse: Place a piece of native copper under or beside a crystal to amplify it, or use it as a conductor in a grid, linking stones with copper wire. Wear a copper bracelet or ring for warmth, and clean it regularly. Hold a native copper nugget during meditation to focus intention. A larger specimen makes an impressive display piece, and many people place it in the southeast corner of the home for flowing energy and abundance.
care: Copper tarnishes in air and moisture, turning brown and then green. Clean raw pieces with a soft dry brush; polished copper jewelry can be wiped with a soft cloth and a mild lemon-and-salt rinse if desired, then dried well. Avoid prolonged water contact. Cleanse with sound, smoke, moonlight or sun. Avoid making elixirs, since copper can leach into liquids, and wash hands after handling raw specimens.
identify: Native copper is orange to brown, soft, heavy and malleable, with a metallic luster and a copper-red streak. Look-alikes include bornite, chalcopyrite and brass. Brass is yellower and harder, while painted rocks or copper-plated stones lack the dendritic form. Many shop pieces are cast or electroformed copper crystals, so ask whether it is natural. Native copper often has a green patina and attached rock.

faq.q: What is native copper used for?
faq.a: In crystal tradition native copper is used as a conductor to amplify stones and move energy, and as a warm, vitalizing stone. It is also worn as jewelry for comfort and connection.
Copper reacts with air and moisture, forming green or blue copper carbonates and chlorides on its surface, called patina. It is a natural process and does not mean the specimen has gone bad.

faq.q: Can I make a copper elixir?
faq.a: No. Copper can leach into water and is not safe for elixirs. Use copper as a display piece or conductor in a grid, and keep it away from drinks and food.
